newsitem.title: JAPAN: Scandal-hit Japan bank says replacing management.
newsitem.headline: Scandal-hit Japan bank says replacing management.

text.p: Scandal-hit Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank (DKB) announced on Tuesday that it would replace its top management with younger executives not tainted by involvement in its illegal loans to a corporate racketeer.
The bank said 21 directors, including current chairman Tadashi Okuda and company president Katsuhiko Kondo, would resign from the company and not take up alternative positions.
It said the directors would be replaced with executives not connected with the scandal.

DKB said 54-year-old managing director Katsuyuki Sugita would become its new president from June 27, rather than vice president Ichiro Fujita, who Kondo had said would succeed him when he announced last month that he would resign to take responsibility for the scandal.

"It is extremely regrettable that the scandal has lowered our credibility as a bank and as a company," DKB said in a statement. Referring to the new management, it said: "We selected individuals who had not been detected to have any involvement in the scandal in our internal investigations."

A source at DKB, which is Japan's second-largest bank in terms of deposits, said the decision was made partly because of on fears of further arrests linked to the bank's loans to a racketeer, a bank source said.
Jiji news agency reported on Tuesday that prosecutors were questioning Fujita over his involvement in the loans.

Last Thursday, prosecutors arrested four DKB officials on suspicion of extending massive uncollateralised loans to Ryuichi Koike, the racketeer at the heart of a scandal which has also ensnared Nomura Securities Co Ltd, Japan's biggest securities house.
Former Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki has also been arrested and prosecutors have questioned former chairman Setsuya Tabuchi and former president Yoshihisa Tabuchi in connection with the scandal.

Nomura went through a similar management upheaval after its racketeer payoffs were revealed, first naming Masashi Suzuki as president and then rescinding the appointment just over a month later to appoint 51-year-old Junichi Ujiie.
Financial analysts have said that the installment of younger, untainted leaders such as Sugita and Ujiie is what the two companies need to win back public trust.

The bank said it will implement management reforms to prevent similar scandals, which will include the setting up of a operations auditing committee. This will consist of members not connected to the bank and will check for any dubious business activities.
